title: Stoic in anger
hook: the jolt, the delay, the other handle

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Attalus, who said memory of lost friends can turn sweet. Your line was grief, honestly.

The email arrives at 4:52 on a Friday. It's from someone who has been difficult all month, and it's passive-aggressive in a way that's almost artistic. A face goes hot. Fingers start moving. Three sharp sentences are written before the email has even been read to the end. A thumb hovers over send. Seneca wrote a long essay on rage, and Epictetus added a tool. Three moves, for the next 4:52 on a Friday.
screen: `4:52 ON A FRIDAY.` → `THREE SHARP SENTENCES.` → `A THUMB OVER SEND.`

segments.voice: First, the jolt. In On Anger, Seneca makes a careful distinction. The hot face, the quickened pulse, the first flare aren't yet anger, he says. They're first movements, like the shiver when cold water splashes you, or a blink when a hand comes near your eyes. They happen to everyone, even the wise. Feeling the jolt isn't failing. Anger begins only when the mind agrees: yes, I've been wronged, and they should pay. That agreement is where you still have a choice. Second, the delay. The greatest remedy for anger, Seneca writes, is delay. Not suppression, just time, so the first heat can cool and the judgment underneath can be looked at. An hour. A night. A walk around the block. The email will still be there. Third, the other handle. Epictetus, in the Handbook, says everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it can't. If your brother wrongs you, don't pick it up by he wronged me; that handle won't carry. Pick it up by he's my brother, we grew up together. With the Friday email: this person is stressed, maybe frightened, maybe having a terrible week. That doesn't excuse them. It just lets you carry the thing without dropping it on your foot. Put together: feel the jolt, delay the reply, find the other handle, then write back. The Monday email is more likely to be shorter, clearer, and something nobody needs to apologize for.
screen: `THE JOLT IS NOT YET ANGER.` · `THE GREATEST REMEDY IS DELAY.` · `PICK IT UP BY THE OTHER HANDLE.` · `JOLT, DELAY, HANDLE, THEN REPLY.` · then, large: `DELAY THE REPLY.`

segments.voice: Recall a recent moment of anger, small enough to look at calmly, and feel for a second the jolt it gave you, heat, tightness, speed, noticing that it simply happened. Imagine a full hour going by, and watch the heat lower a little. Then look for the other handle: what else is true about this person, and what might they be carrying?
On Anger, Seneca's essay where the first hot jolt is not yet anger, only a first movement, until the mind agrees you've been wronged. Today's word.
Your line: delay the reply. The jolt is yours to feel; the answer can wait. Day six hundred eighty, done.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat the first flare of anger as involuntary, wait before replying, and then deliberately look for a more charitable way to see the other person.
